prize_parts.citation: for credible empirical evidence on how technology and international trade reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B037 remains my first choice, but my configuration has changed: the third name is now Dorn, not Katz. The chair asked whether the technology and task strand and the import-shock strand are one discovery, and the exchange has persuaded me to define the achievement more narrowly. I now read it as design-based evidence, using local labour markets, on how technology and trade shocks change labour demand, wages and adjustment. On that reading Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the natural set. The import-shock papers are jointly authored by the three. From my recollection, which I have not verified, Autor and Dorn's work on polarisation and low-skill service jobs also uses local labour markets. If that is right, Dorn spans both strands as a co-author, and the set does not leave the technology side resting on Autor alone. That answers the concern I raised in round 1. The Katz-versus-Dorn choice is also easier to defend on overlap grounds. Katz's skill-premium work is foundational, and the committee would honour it by recognising the long-run framework. But that is the ground closest to the 2023 prize, and I now judge it a thematically distinct and older contribution that does not need to be bundled in. The claim is general. Adjustment to technology and trade is slow, uneven and concentrated in particular places, and this is a lesson about how economies work, not about one dataset. The designs are transparent, they have been replicated in other countries, and they have been refined rather than overturned. The core papers are a decade or more old, which is enough time for scrutiny. The ongoing debate over magnitudes is what a mature programme looks like. The citation should be worded around credible evidence on adjustment and should not assert settled welfare totals or originate the whole task framework.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is still a composite. Dropping Katz leaves out the long-run education-versus-technology framing, and the citation then honours the technology strand mainly through Autor and Dorn's empirical work, not through the earliest conceptual contributions. Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane have claims on the task framework that the credited set does not cover. Subject adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes is a risk even if I judge the discoveries distinct. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the robustness of shift-share instruments, are still contested. A narrower prize also invites the objection that it rewards the more contested strand. Finally, I work in this part of the field and have changed my third name in the same direction as the chair and Dreber, so I should not treat that convergence as independent evidence.

responses.point: Hassler moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson on the grounds that the trade-shock strand has the cleanest credit. He prefers Dorn to Katz because of overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. He keeps the technology strand in the citation through Autor and concedes that the choice leaves out the long-run education-versus-technology framing.
responses.response: In round 1 I defended Katz because I thought dropping him left technology resting on Autor alone. Your argument that Autor carries the task and polarisation evidence is stronger than I credited, and I now add that Dorn is a co-author of the local-labour-market polarisation work as well. I have moved to your trio. I do not accept that overlap is the deciding factor. Goldin's prize concerned long-run gender and education evidence, so the overlap with Katz is thematic and not substantive. My reason for the change is that one coherent discovery, evidence from local labour markets on technology and trade, needs Dorn more than it needs Katz. I agree with you that the cost, omitting the skill-premium framing, should be stated openly.

responses.point: Enflo prefers Autor, Hanson and Katz because the three span both strands. She regards Dorn in place of Katz as a defensible variant and would move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee decides the prize should honour only the trade-shock design. She also says the composite problem is not disqualifying because both strands share one object, the changing demand for labour.
responses.response: I have moved toward your fallback, but for a reason that differs slightly from yours. I still think the two strands share one object. I now think the more coherent way to honour that object is through the local-labour-market evidence, not through a framework whose originators are spread across Katz, Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu. That is why I do not describe the Dorn trio as a trade-only prize, though I accept the citation then rests on evidence and not on the framework. You noted that I would hold that Katz's case is not stronger on the China-shock evidence. I agree. His claim rests on the earlier skill-premium work, which is real. If you think that work needs to be in the citation, we disagree. Because Katz's work is foundational, I would not call omitting him costless.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson keeps Katz so that the prize credits both the labour-demand framework and the trade-shock evidence. She calls this not clearly right and says the cleaner trio is the trade-shock one if colleagues judge the strands separable. She also argues that the 2023 and 2024 prizes did not cite the demand-side account of technology and trade, so the discovery is not already recognised.
responses.response: I agree with your second point and I disagree with the claim that adjacency should lower B037. The 2023 and 2024 prizes did not address this demand-side question, and I do not want my change of third name read as conceding that. My change comes from the chair's question about one discovery or two. I now judge that the discovery is best defined by its evidence and that Katz's contribution, though foundational, is a separable earlier one. You are right that this is a judgement and not a scientific finding. I take seriously the cost to the framework strand. If the committee prefers to credit both strands explicitly, your set is the right one, and I would not oppose it on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Friberg treats B037 as an alternative, proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn, and keeps B022 as his preferred configuration. He notes that the trade-shock strand is cleanly attributed. He also says the long-run interpretation is contested, which makes the timing somewhat less mature than for the leading candidates, and that the two strands may be bundled.
responses.response: I have adopted your trio. I still think the maturity concern is manageable. The designs have been replicated across countries, and the disputes concern magnitude and persistence, not whether adjustment costs exist. That is a reason to word the citation around evidence on adjustment. I do not think it justifies waiting. On B022 against B037, I would not hold B022 to a lower standard because it is a method. BLP changed what can be measured, and its attribution is cleaner than many of ours. My preference for B037 rests on the replicated, design-based evidence about an economic phenomenon, and its limits on magnitudes are in the open. Whether a committee prefers a method that changed practice to a body of evidence that changed a policy debate is a real difference of standard, and I do not claim to settle it.

responses.point: Teorell holds that B045 is a unified theory-plus-evidence programme and distinct from the 2024 prize, since it concerns how specific rules shape policy choices within a country. He accepts that identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence is weaker and that the committee could still weigh the adjacency differently. He answered my round-1 identification point by arguing that the unifying contribution is the framework and that the empirical work tests its predictions.
responses.response: The chair asked what would change my concern about B045. I accept your distinction from 2024 as stated: rules within a polity are a different question from colonial institutions and long-run prosperity. My concern is mainly identification. I would move B045 up if the committee could point to credibly identified, replicated evidence, for example from within-country variation in electoral rules or accountability, that confirms the framework's central predictions and does not rely on cross-country correlations. I have not seen that case argued in the exchange. I also agree with you and Strömberg that a Persson-Tabellini pair would be sharper than a trio. I keep B045 outside my alternatives, because B001 and B004 have clearer attribution and I weigh that more heavily here.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology and trade-shock strands as one discovery defined by local-labour-market evidence or as two, in which case Katz's skill-premium framework would need to be credited explicitly.

Whether my recollection that Autor and Dorn's polarisation work uses local labour markets is accurate. I have not checked the papers, and the Dorn trio relies on this point to cover the technology strand.
How large and persistent the China-shock effects were, and how robust shift-share designs and task measures are.
Whether adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes should reduce the weight given to B037. I judge the discoveries distinct but cannot rule out that others will not.
Whether Autor and Hanson alone would be the cleaner attribution if the committee cannot agree on a third name. I would accept it as a fallback.
I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the round-1 files, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. The supplied profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz. I am an empirical labour economist in the credibility tradition, and B037 is close to my field, so I may weigh identification credibility more heavily than others do. I have applied the same criteria to all fields. My shift from Katz to Dorn follows the chair's question and colleagues' arguments and does not rest on any personal tie. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
